notes: Interpolation convention between data points: linear-inclusive (numpy/R7), nearest-rank (ceil), exclusive (Excel .EXC/R6), Hazen (MATLAB/R5), or round-to-nearest index — all give different answers for e.g. p=25 on [1,2,3,4].
Empty list: raise ValueError vs return math.nan.
p outside [0,100]: raise ValueError vs silently clamp to [0,100].
Exclusive and Hazen methods produce ranks outside 1..n near p=0/100 and must clamp to min/max, so they saturate earlier than the inclusive method (e.g. p=90 on 5 items).
Nearest-rank uses ceil, so p=0 needs a special case to return the minimum rather than an out-of-range index.
Round-to-nearest uses Python's banker's rounding (round(1.5)==2, round(0.5)==0), which is deterministic but surprising at exact .5 ranks.
Order of validation matters: one candidate checks p before checking emptiness, so ([], 101) raises rather than returning nan.
